extracted.intended_audience: registered patent and trademark practitioners (U.S. attorneys) who practice before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, rules, and remedial requirements governing practitioner conduct before the USPTO (with emphasis on trademark matters), including signature and U.S. counsel requirements, ethical duties, sanctions, suspension duties, and reinstatement conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (Requirement of U.S. licensed attorney for foreign-domiciled trademark applicants/registrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants, registrants, or parties to a trademark proceeding whose domicile is not located within the U.S. or its territories must be represented by an attorney who is an active member in good standing of the bar of the highest court of a state in the U.S. (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a); 84 FR 31498).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective August 3, 2019. Intended to reduce unauthorized practice of law (UPL), improve accuracy of submissions, and safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark register. Practitioners representing applicants are expected to undertake bona fide review of specimens and ensure compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations. Failure to comply can jeopardize registrations and violate USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (personal electronic signatures required)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; an electronically signing person must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature and placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission. (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a),(c); 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties (paralegals, assistants, secretaries) may not sign for the named signatory. Typing another person’s electronic signature does not constitute a valid signature. TMEP § 611.01(c) and case authorities (In re Dermahose; In re Cowan) reinforce this proscription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations under penalty of perjury and criminal exposure for false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications contain declarations signed under penalty of perjury; false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. § 1001. Signatories make specific representations regarding use of marks in commerce or intent to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO relies on such declarations during examination and issuance of registrations; improper or impermissible signatures on declarations can jeopardize the client’s intellectual property rights and expose the signatory to legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of competence and knowledge of client identity (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation and know who the client is, taking reasonable steps to avoid foreseeable prejudice to the rights of the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with foreign intermediaries, the trademark applicant is the client; receiving instructions through a foreign agent does not change client identity (see responsibilities guidance and Strojirenstvi v. Toyoda). Practitioners must understand applicable USPTO rules (e.g., U.S. Counsel Rule, signature rules) relevant to representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes ensuring that clients’ trademark filings are prepared, reviewed, signed, and filed in compliance with the U.S. Counsel Rule and USPTO signature requirements. Failure to take reasonable steps can constitute a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must inform clients about matters reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically includes informing clients of actual or potential adverse consequences of noncompliance with the U.S. Counsel Rule and signature rules (e.g., whether impermissible electronic signing jeopardizes IP rights), so clients can make informed decisions about their applications or registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.303)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must be candid toward the USPTO and must not knowingly make false statements or authorize false filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowingly authorizing a third party to sign the practitioner’s name on trademark documents (including declarations) violates candor obligations. Subsections cited include (a)(1), (a)(3), (b), and (d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistance (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must supervise and is responsible for the conduct of non-practitioner assistants to the extent required by the rules; must not authorize non-practitioners to sign for the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorizing a non-practitioner to insert the practitioner’s electronic signature on documents (including declarations) filed with the USPTO where the non-practitioner prepared, signed, and filed documents breaches this responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting others in unauthorized practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not assist non-practitioners in practicing before the USPTO in trademark matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes permitting third-party non-practitioners to prepare, consult on, sign, and file USPTO filings without the practitioner’s supervision. Such assistance constitutes facilitating unauthorized practice and is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the U.S. trademark registration system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that undermines the integrity of the trademark registration system is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include noncompliance with the U.S. Counsel Rule, failure to follow signature requirements, and assisting others to engage in unauthorized practice; such conduct can prejudice the trademark register’s accuracy and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide bar information when representing clients (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.17(b)(3), 2.32(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. attorneys are required to provide their bar information to the USPTO when representing applicants and registrants, whether domiciled inside or outside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aids USPTO oversight and enforcement of the U.S. Counsel Rule and practitioner accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP § 611.01(c) explicit guidance on signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: TMEP guidance states that all documents must be personally signed and the person identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature; another person may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterates that typing another person’s electronic signature is not a valid signature, analogous to signing someone’s name on paper; violations can lead to disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to take corrective action for harm caused by improper filings
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who discovers improper filings or impermissible signatures must take appropriate corrective actions to remediate potential harm to clients’ intellectual property rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of corrective actions taken by Respondent: terminating the business relationship, restricting third-party access to correspondence email, contacting affected clients to inform them and taking corrective action at no charge when authorized, contacting the USPTO regarding improper filings, and notifying successor counsel where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions imposed for violations (suspension and probation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanctions may include suspension from practice before the Office for a specified period and a probationary period with conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this matter Respondent agreed to a 30-day suspension commencing 14 days after the Final Order, plus a 12‑month probationary period with specific conditions. Failure to comply with probation can trigger an Order to Show Cause and possible additional suspension up to 11 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probationary compliance conditions (CLE, review of rules, monitoring, reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific probation conditions can require continuing legal education, rule/manual review, monitoring of USPTO records, and periodic reporting to OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: complete six (6) hours CLE (2 hours ethics/professional responsibility; 4 hours U.S. trademark law); review TMEP (including signature requirements), 37 C.F.R. § 2.11, and 84 FR commentary; weekly searches of TESS for applications naming the practitioner and prompt notification to USPTO for unauthorized filings; quarterly written reports to OED certifying completion of searches and findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order to Show Cause and additional discipline procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED believes the practitioner failed to comply with probation conditions or rules, OED will issue an Order to Show Cause giving the practitioner 15 days to respond; OED may then request the USPTO Director to enter an order suspending the practitioner for up to an additional 11 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure includes delivery of the Order, response period, and submission of argument/evidence to USPTO Director. Review by the practitioner of such action does not stay an imposed suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties during suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended practitioner has specific duties: notify jurisdictions and agencies to which admitted, notify clients with immediate or prospective business before the Office (including urgent dates), notify opposing parties/practitioners in pending matters, and refrain from holding out or rendering services before the Office until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: 37 C.F.R. § 11.58(c)(2)-(4), (b)(2), (b)(5). Notifications must specify urgent dates and advise clients to seek other counsel if not represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of compliance after suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must provide an affidavit of compliance certifying compliance with the Order, with appended copies of notices sent, names and addresses of recipients, and return receipts or returned mail, and a list of jurisdictions to which notice was sent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The affidavit need not append banking schedules or certain other financial schedules and need not append an affidavit describing steps to remove advertising unless specified. See §11.58(d)(1)-(5) for specifics on required and not-required appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition not available during short-term suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the suspension commences 14 days after entry, the practitioner shall not be granted limited recognition under § 11.58(f) during the suspension period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited recognition provisions do not excuse compliance with suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition for reinstatement requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not resume practice before the Office until reinstated by order of OED Director or USPTO Director and must file a petition for reinstatement complying with § 11.60(c) and accompanied by the required fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition must attest compliance with § 11.58(a) (including sworn declaration that practitioner did not practice before the Office during suspension) and satisfy other §11.60(c)(1)-(3) requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of disciplinary actions and public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Orders and disciplinary decisions are to be electronically published by OED (FOIA Reading Room) and a notice is to be published in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication includes a summary notice of suspension and probation and the grounds for discipline, making disciplinary history public and available for future consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary record as aggravating factor in future proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may consider the record of this disciplinary proceeding in later proceedings regarding the same or similar misconduct as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations by the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in the Final Order prevents the Office from using this record in future disciplinary actions or proceedings; the record may affect discipline severity later.
